description: We are a team of three students working on a project called Lunar Landing Site Navigator. We are interested in space exploration, programming, and innovative technologies. Our goal is to develop a solution that helps identify and evaluate safe landing sites on the Moon. We are looking for motivated teammates with skills in programming, data analysis, scientific research, or UI/UX design. We value creativity, responsibility, and teamwork.
summary:
Near the lunar south pole the Sun and the Earth stay close to the horizon, so whether a lander gets power and a line of sight home depends on the real terrain around the exact landing point, on the dates and on how high its panel and antenna stand. Our web tool answers the engineering question directly: for 15 candidate sites (Artemis III regions, LOLA site models, IM-2) and any dates in 2027-2029 it shows when the Sun and the Earth are above the terrain horizon, simulates a lander's battery hour by hour, gives a verdict — survives or not — and the smallest battery that survives,
compares sites, finds the best landing days for a mission, and shows how much a mast of 2 to 20 m.
helps. Terrain comes from LOLA elevation models, Sun and Earth positions from NASA's SPICE toolkit;
both were checked against JPL Horizons and the published LOLA illumination maps.
details:
What it does. Six pages: Site & dates (map, horizon panorama with the Sun and Earth paths, timeline of light and link, statistics); Power (sliders for panel, battery and loads; verdict; battery needed and its mass); Mast trade-off (light, longest night, battery and Earth link versus mast height, and where the gain levels off); Compare sites; Landing windows (calendar of every landing day and the five best); Methods & data.

How it works. An offline pipeline traces the terrain horizon of each site and mast height along 720 azimuths over 300 km of LOLA terrain (5 m models near the site, 40 m beyond) with exact spherical geometry, and stores the apparent Sun and Earth positions for 2027-2029 from the DE440 ephemeris (SPICE, light time and aberration, in the lunar frame of the terrain). The app computes the visible share of each disc above the horizon, an hourly energy balance of panel, battery and loads, and Earth-link windows by a chosen rule. The smallest battery that survives is solved exactly. Everything the app needs fits in 3.6 MB; a parameter change is recomputed in well under a second.

Results (default lander, 2027). At Connecting Ridge a 10 m mast instead of 2 m raises the time with sunlight from 79.1 % to 95.1 % and cuts the battery needed for the year from 51.5 kWh to 5.1 kWh; the gain levels off at about 10 m at ridge sites, while at Haworth a mast hardly helps. At Malapert Massif the mast also raises the time with the Earth in view from 62.7 % to 89.1 % (2 to 20 m). The best landing days keep both the Sun and the Earth in view for a whole 14-day mission.

Benefits and intended impact. Mission and lander engineers get a quick, transparent first answer to "will it survive here and then?" and to the mast-or-battery trade-off, with every assumption listed and every placeholder marked, before running detailed thermal and power analyses.

Validation. Sun and Earth directions agree with JPL Horizons to 0.00003°; the Sun elevation at the Apollo 11 landing is 10.70° (Horizons 10.70°, mission plan 10.8°); our 18.6-year visibility statistics agree with the published LOLA maps within 2.7 points (Sun) and 0.8 points (Earth) on average around four sites; the longest sunlit spells in the 2027-2029 midsummers agree with the peer-reviewed model of Wueller et al. (2026) within 1 day for 32 of 36 site-years; horizon peaks land on the real massifs in LROC camera images. 287 automated tests.

Limits. A visible Sun is not yet power and a visible Earth is not yet a radio link; dust, temperatures, the lander's shadow, station schedules and relays are not modelled. The lander power values follow a NASA reference lander, a solar-cell datasheet and a textbook sizing calculation; no engineer has reviewed them.

Tools. Python, NumPy, pandas, PyArrow, rasterio, SpiceyPy (NAIF SPICE), Streamlit, Plotly, Matplotlib, pytest, uv; Claude Code.

Team. COSMOSMARTES: Hadiyatullo Ibrohimov, Zikrullo Asrorov, Umarkhon Hamdamov.
